Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Discuss the influence of **ONE** active factor on soil formation.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Soil formation (pedogenesis) results from the interaction of five factors. The **passive factors** (parent material, relief and time) are the materials and conditions on which the soil forms; the **active factors** (**climate** and **organisms**, vegetation and animals included) are the forces that act on them and make the changes. The active factor discussed here is **climate**, through its two elements, temperature and precipitation.

**1. Climate controls the speed and the type of weathering of the parent material.**
- **Temperature.** Chemical reactions are faster in the heat (roughly doubling for each rise of 10 °C). In hot humid regions chemical weathering is very rapid, so the parent rock is broken down to a depth of tens of metres. In cold regions, weathering is mainly physical (frost shattering) and slow, so soils are thin and stony.
- **Water.** Rainfall supplies the water that dissolves and hydrolyses the minerals, and makes the soil solution that supports plant life.

**2. Climate controls the movement of materials in the soil.**
- Where rainfall is higher than evaporation, water moves downwards and **leaches** soluble bases (calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium), and silica, out of the upper horizons. In the strongly leached equatorial soils iron and aluminium oxides remain behind (**laterisation**), giving a red, deep, acid **ferrallitic soil** low in nutrients, as under the rainforest of southern Cameroon. In cool humid climates the leaching under coniferous litter produces a **podzol** with a grey leached E horizon.
- Where evaporation is higher than rainfall (the dry tropical and the semi-arid areas) the water moves upwards by capillarity and salts and lime accumulate near the surface (**calcification, salinisation**), giving soils that are shallow, rich in bases and alkaline, as in the Sahelian margin.

**3. Climate controls the organic matter and the vegetation.**
- Climate decides the vegetation (forest, savanna, grassland) and so the amount and the quality of the litter. In the hot humid forest, decomposition by bacteria and fungi is so fast that humus does not accumulate and the nutrients are held in the vegetation (rapid nutrient cycling). In the cool climates, decomposition is slow and an acid raw humus accumulates (peat or mor). In temperate grassland areas, moderate rainfall and temperature give deep, dark, humus-rich soils such as chernozems.
- Rain also controls the depth of the profile and the differentiation of horizons (eluviation and illuviation).

**Evaluation.** Climate is the dominant factor over large areas: the great zonal soil types of the world (ferrallitic, ferruginous, desert, chernozem, podzol) follow the climate zones. Its effect is, however, modified by the parent material, the relief (drainage, erosion) and by time (it takes a long time for a deep profile to develop), and by the vegetation which is itself a product of climate. *(Alternative answer: organisms, discussing the roles of vegetation litter and humus, soil fauna such as earthworms and termites, microbes and human activity.)*

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) How would you ensure the conservation of a forest or grassland ecosystem in your community?

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Conservation** means the wise use of an ecosystem so that it continues to yield its benefits (timber, fuel, food, water protection, soil protection, biodiversity, climate regulation) for present and future generations. The answer is given for a **forest ecosystem** (the measures for a grassland are added in the last paragraph); the candidate should relate it to his or her own community (for example a village in the forest zone, or a savanna community).

**Measures to conserve a forest ecosystem**

1. **Laws, protected areas and their enforcement.** Establish and protect forest reserves, national parks and sanctuaries (for example Korup National Park and the Dja Faunal Reserve in Cameroon), apply the forestry law (permits, quotas, fines and prison sentences for illegal logging and poaching) and have forest guards who patrol and monitor, aided by satellite images and mobile phone reports.
2. **Community participation.** Involve the people who live in the forest: **community forests**, forest management committees which share the benefits (a part of the forest revenue and employment) so that the people have an interest in protecting the forest, and the respect of customary rules and sacred groves.
3. **Sustainable logging.** Allow only **selective** felling of mature trees by a management plan, with a **rotation** (a long cutting cycle), the felling of trees above a minimum diameter, the protection of seed trees, less-damaging methods (directional felling, fewer logging roads), **replanting** and the use of certified timber.
4. **Reforestation and afforestation.** Plant trees in cleared and degraded areas, in nurseries run by the school or by the village, and establish **woodlots** and fast-growing species for fuelwood, so that the natural forest is not cut for fuel.
5. **Better farming and alternatives.** Teach and encourage **agroforestry**, permanent cultivation with improved seeds and fertiliser in place of slash-and-burn, the intensification of farming on the land already cleared, **fire control**, and alternatives to fuelwood and bushmeat (improved stoves, cooking gas, solar energy, the breeding of animals such as cane rats and snails).
6. **Education and sensitisation.** Campaigns in the schools, the churches, the media and the markets on the value of forests, the fight against bushfires and poaching, and the development of **ecotourism** and of non-timber forest products (honey, mushrooms, medicinal plants, spices) that bring income without destroying the forest.
7. **International help.** Cooperation and funding (for example the programmes that pay for reduced deforestation such as REDD+, and the agreements of the Congo basin countries).

**For a grassland (savanna) ecosystem:** control of **bush burning** (early, controlled burning), controlled and rotational **grazing** and the limitation of the number of livestock to the carrying capacity, creation of grazing reserves and water points spread out, reseeding and protection of the vegetation against over-grazing and fuelwood cutting, protection of wildlife in parks (for example Waza National Park) and laws against poaching.

**Conclusion.** The conservation of an ecosystem succeeds only if the law, the local people's interests and the use of alternatives are combined: the aim is sustainable use and not the complete exclusion of the people.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Explain why the main soil type in the Diamare plain of the Northern Lowlands is more fertile than the main soil type in the South Cameroon Low Plateau.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The soils compared.**

- The Diamare plain (and the flat lowlands of the Logone and the Benue) is covered with **young alluvial soils and dark clay soils (vertisols, called "karal" locally)**, together with ferruginous (tropical iron-rich) soils on the slightly higher ground. These are formed from fine **alluvial and lacustrine deposits** laid down by the rivers (the mayos) and the floods.
- The South Cameroon Low Plateau has deep, red-yellow **ferrallitic (lateritic) soils** formed by the intense weathering of the old crystalline basement rocks under the hot, wet equatorial climate and the rainforest.

**Why the Diamare soil is more fertile.**

1. **Lower rainfall and less leaching.** The Diamare receives only about 600 to 900 mm of rain, all in 4 to 5 months, followed by a long dry season. The soil water moves upwards for most of the year, so the soluble **bases (calcium, magnesium, potassium)** are not removed. On the plateau, the rainfall is 1500 to 2000 mm or more in nearly all the months, so the nutrients are strongly **leached** down beyond the roots of crops (the soil is "washed out").
2. **Young soils, formed from fresh minerals.** The Diamare soils are formed from alluvium that is rich in minerals, and the yearly floods of the rivers **add fresh silt** and bring in nutrients again. The plateau soils are very old and have been weathered for millions of years; most of the weatherable minerals have been destroyed, so that no new nutrients are released.
3. **Type of clay and nutrient retention.** The clay in the Diamare vertisols is of the **montmorillonite (smectite)** type, which has a high cation exchange capacity, so it holds the nutrients and the water well. The plateau soils contain **kaolinite and iron and aluminium oxides**, with a very low capacity to store nutrients, and they are acid with a tendency to fix phosphorus and with some aluminium toxicity.
4. **Silica and the remaining minerals.** The strong leaching on the plateau removes the silica and the bases and leaves the **oxides of iron and aluminium** (laterite), which give a red colour and make the soil acid and poor. In the Diamare the soil is neutral to slightly alkaline.
5. **Water holding capacity.** The heavy clay of the karal holds water for a long time, which allows the cultivation of dry-season sorghum (muskuwaari) after the rains, whereas the plateau soils are generally well drained and the nutrients are lost with the water.
6. **Humus and nutrient cycling.** On the plateau, most of the nutrients are in the living forest biomass and in the thin humus layer, as the bacteria decompose the litter very quickly in the heat; if the forest is cleared the humus and nutrients are rapidly lost and the fertility declines within 2 or 3 years (hence shifting cultivation). In the drier Diamare the vegetation litter decomposes slowly and the humus is kept in the soil.

**Qualification.** The Diamare soils also have problems: hard clay that is difficult to work when it is dry and sticky when wet, risks of drought, and erosion and degradation (bare "harde" soils) caused by overgrazing; and the plateau soils support dense forest and valuable crops (cocoa, oil palm) through the closed nutrient cycle. In terms of the **natural chemical fertility**, however, the Diamare soil is richer.
